The '''Niuatoputapu languague''' ([[Tongan language|Tongan]]: ''Lea Faka-Niuatoputapu'') was a [[Polynesian languages|Polynesian language]] and the indigenous language of the people of [[Niuatoputapu|Niuatoputapu, Tonga]] and possibly [[Tafahi|Tafahi, Tonga]] due to its close proximity. Sometime between the 18th to 19th century, it became extinct and its use was replaced by modern Tongan ([[Tongan language|Tongan]]: ''Lea Faka-Tonga''), although small remnants of the old Niuatoputapu language can still be heard in the Tongan language spoken on Niuatoputapu and Tafahi today, as well as in the islands' geographic features. For example, the islet of Nukuseilala (''Land of the [[Garcinia sessilis|Seilala Tree]]'') appears to use the old Niuatoputapu and modern Samoan pronunciation of "seilala" instead of the modern Tongan "heilala".

The Niuatoputapu language is believed to have been very distinct from the modern [[Tongan language|Tongan]] and [[Niuafoʻou language|Niuafoʻou]] languages, being closely related instead to [[Samoan language|Samoan]], [[Futunan language|East Futunan]], [[Tokelauan language|Tokelauan]], [[Tuvaluan language|Tuvaluan]] and [[Pukapukan language|Pukapukan]].

Practically all knowledge of the Niuatoputapu language comes from a word list of 32 words compiled by [[Jacob Le Maire]] in 1616 after visits to both Niuatoputapu and Tafahi.<ref>[http://www2.ling.su.se/pollinet/facts/ntp.html "Niuatoputapu - Languages facts sheet by Niklas Jonsson"], Niklas Jonsson, 16 December 1998</ref>

==Phonology==

=== Vowels ===
The Niuatoputapu language, as with other Polynesian languages, is believed to have had five vowels with both long and short forms. On their own, each vowel is considered a [[monophthong]].

Also similarly to other Polynesian languages, certain pairings of monophthongs may be used to form a corresponding [[diphthong]], with common examples including ae, ai, ao, au, ou, and ei. 

=== Consonants ===
The 10 known consonants of the Niuatoputapu language, plus possible usage of the glottal stop, are gathered from Le Maire's wordlist recorded in 1616 and parts of the language still in local use. These match very closely with the Futunan language.

==Comparison with Futunan==
Shortly after visiting Niuatoputapu and Tafahi islands, Le Maire and his expedition continued on to [[Futuna (Wallis and Futuna)|Futuna]] and [[Alofi Island|Alofi]] islands of modern-day [[Wallis and Futuna]] where he recorded a larger list of words from the local [[Futunan language]] (Futunan: ''Le Māsau Fakafutuna'') which is still spoken today. As the Futunan language is still in popular use in the 21st century, the Niuatoputapu and Futunan languages are believed to have been very close to each other, and both wordlists from Le Maire were collected within a short period of time, the Futunan language is able to offer perspective on the known aspects of the Niuatoputapu language and how they might look or might have sounded like.
